prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made quantum-state control and clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level reproducible across laboratories

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a stand-alone prize to Katori and Ye. In answer to the chair's first question, here is the one sentence I would defend: the lattice clock is the invention of a trapping scheme in which a magic wavelength removes the light shift of the clock transition while thousands of neutral atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so that statistical power and systematic control are obtained together. The comb (2005) gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems. Neither gave an ensemble clock whose atoms are controlled well enough that, with 1e-18 comparisons, one sees a gravitational redshift across a millimetre and the first signs of many-body effects in the clock itself. That is a new regime of quantum control of matter, and I count it as physics and not only as instrumentation. What persuades me most is independent reproduction in JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and NPL, not any single group's record. The two-name credit follows the history as I understand it: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and coherence limits and for the many-body clock. I do not see a case for a third name that is strong enough to displace either of them, and I would not want to spend the third slot on a second part with no common thread.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take seriously are the same as before, and I have not found a decisive answer to all of them. First, precedent: the 2005 and 2012 prizes sit close, and a purist can say this is the third prize on precision measurement. Second, credit: Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto made real contributions and the early Tokyo versus JILA priority history is not something I can settle from my own knowledge. Third, the redefinition of the second has not been adopted; I regard it as a procedural matter, but a skeptic can call the case prospective. Fourth, I am a theorist near this field through quantum technology and I cannot rule out that I am too generous to a clean measurement story. Against the alternatives: B061 has the more contestable credit because Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe, and B028 is a single-name discovery whose mechanism is still unexplained and which does not fit with an atomic-physics clock as a shared prize.

responses.point: The chair asked Kroll and Lindroth for draft citation wording and for a clear statement of why the lattice clock is a distinct invention. Kroll's round-1 case rests on magic-wavelength trapping with many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, intercompared across national laboratories.
responses.response: I have built my citation on your formulation, but I have tried to make the wording say what is new: the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting control of an ensemble, not only a lower number. I would avoid wording such as 'better than the microwave second', which turns the prize into a metrology milestone and invites the comparison with 2005 and 2012. I also accept your point that the redefinition of the second is a matter of procedure and not of whether the physics works, and I agree that it should not make us wait. Where I would press you is the Wineland-group Al+ ion clocks that held the accuracy record for a time: the committee should be ready to say that the lattice clock outperforms them in stability because of the number of atoms, and that this is an invention in its own right and not a competing record.

responses.point: Olsson, with Danielsson, pairs B040 with Hosono's iron-based superconductors (B028) as two separate, mature, cleanly credited achievements, three people in total.
responses.response: I respect the cleanliness of Hosono's credit and I have kept B028 on my list of alternatives for that reason. The observation of superconductivity in LaFeAsO was a real surprise and was confirmed within weeks. But I do not think a two-part prize should be put together to reach a shape. You and Danielsson both concede there is no common thread, and the chair notes the other supporters of B028 are few. Condensed-matter materials are also outside my own competence, so I defer to you on the materials details, but I cannot see that the lattice clock gains in strength by the pairing. If the committee wants a second part, I would sooner ask whether the pairing mechanism, the early Tc increases by other groups and the Kamihara question make the citation wording difficult; my reading is that they do, and that the single-part prize is the more defensible final position.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B040 low at opening, then moved to it, and still calls the lattice clock to some an instrument and not a discovery, with the risk of a third helping from the same dish as 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take the instrument-versus-discovery objection to be the most serious scientific one, and I do not dismiss it. My answer is that the lattice clock did more than improve a number: it changed what can be measured. Differences in the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, bounds on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and spin-exchange and many-body effects in degenerate Fermi gases were not accessible before. A further test is whether other fields use it as a tool for physics; they do. I would also like to hear whether Danielsson's reservation is about the physics or the precedent. If it is precedent alone, I think the 2005 and 2012 prizes honour different advances, and I do not find the 'third helping' reading compelling. I would nevertheless accept that Danielsson's concern about pairing with an unrelated part is a fair reason to prefer the stand-alone version.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B061 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a stand-alone prize, says it is arguably overdue, and treats B040 as the better-attributed fallback if the credit cannot be drawn cleanly.
responses.response: I agree that B061 is a strong piece of physics: a new class of matter, the Z2 invariant, and a clean quantised conductance experiment with two decades of confirmation. As in round 1, my concern is credit, not science. The HgTe proposal that Molenkamp measured is due to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and with the three-name limit I do not see a citation that fixes this without dropping someone. Eriksson thinks the wording can handle the gap; I am not convinced that a citation can describe an observation without crediting the prediction that told the experimentalists where to look. You say B040 is your fallback if the credit cannot be drawn. My view is that it cannot, and I hope that on that reading you will join B040 in the final ballot, while I keep B061 as my first alternative should the committee decide otherwise.

uncertainties: Whether Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemonde or other lattice-clock contributors have a claim comparable to Katori or Ye, and what the external expert reports say on early Tokyo versus JILA priority.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention and a new regime of quantum control, or reads it as the next increment after the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a stand-alone prize is better than a second part, and whether B028 would hold up against the unexplained pairing mechanism and the credit for Kamihara and the early Tc increases.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay a decision, which I think it should not.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, a national programme built on superconducting circuits, and am close to the circuit QED community concerned by B055; I recuse myself from any decision on B055 and keep it out of my configuration. I know of no specific tie to Katori, Ye, Hosono or the topological-insulator candidates. WACQT has links to AMO and quantum-sensing groups at Lund, and Chalmers colleagues work on precision measurement, but I have no collaboration with the clock groups and no institutional stake in B040.
